one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the companion column to B15 -- last Sunday's three-hotspots survey -- by zooming out to historical arcs and strategic options. Since time immemorial, humankind has been torn by strife and war: beginning among families and tribes, then crossing nations as humans mastered the earth and its resources, with victors enslaving the vanquished, raping their women, plundering their land, and looting their treasury. Weak nations paid tribute to the strong. Pax Romana reigned only while Rome remained absolutely supreme. The recurring cycle continued until the end of World War I when the victors formed the League of Nations as multiparty guarantor of world peace -- which utterly failed within two decades because it had no power to sanction violators, allowing Hitler to rise riding the Nazi rhetoric of condemning the harsh WWI surrender terms that impoverished Germans. After WWII the allied powers learned their lesson: instead of totally impoverishing the vanquished with heavy reparations, the US-led victors assisted them to recover through the Marshall Plan and MacArthur Plan (to rebuild Japan); Germany and Japan now lead Europe and Asia (except China) in economic development and have become America's great allies. The UN was equipped with more teeth, except that sanctions only work if the five victors (US, Russia, UK, France, China) who constitute the permanent SC members are unanimous -- any veto defeats a UN sanction. Consequently, the United States, sometimes by its lonesome or with token aid from its allies, became the sole guarantor of peace: Pax Americana reigned because American arms and men intervened in regional aggressions, as in Korea and Vietnam. But it was not absolutely successful: US-led UN forces protected South Korea's territorial integrity but were not able to sanction the North Korean invaders (assisted by China) who retained their half of the 38th parallel; America was defeated by a defiant North Vietnam (though united Vietnam paradoxically became a US ally in the SCS dispute); the war-on-terror record in Iraq and Afghanistan has been spotty; rising casualties and costs have made America war-weary, to the utter dismay of old allies like Saudi Arabia and Israel. In the face of current threats in the three hotspots (SCS/East China Sea, Ukraine, Middle East) and a fourth suggested by readers (India-Pakistan), the US resolve to maintain Pax Americana is being put to severe test. The crucial question faces the American people who will soon elect a new president: will they continue bearing the high human and economic costs of being the world's policeman? Will they prevent World War III? Will they escape its devastation if it happens? The best way of preventing a nuclear war is to destroy all nuclear weapons -- the US and Russia tried, but other nations did not follow suit and in fact acquired their own atomic arsenals; so the strategy has gone back to aiming for peace but bracing for war. Traditional war-avoidance modes include diplomacy, negotiations, good offices, conciliation, arbitration, boycott, embargo, and blockade. Ironically, however, the real deterrent to a misbehaving nuclear power is the threat of mutual annihilation, as shown by President Kennedy in 1962 when he made clear the US was prepared for Armageddon if Khrushchev did not recall the nuclear-arms-carrying Soviet ships steaming toward Cuba. World War III would mean veritable destruction of all combatants; while America escaped direct devastation in WWI and WWII, it cannot avoid the nuclear fallout of its own ICBMs, not to count the warheads flung by its enemies. Ideally, CJP believes the real guarantee of world peace is the rule of law -- humans conquered the earth not because of brutal muscles of lions and bears or teeth of sharks, but because of their intelligence and reason; only by the same rationality through faithful observance of the rule of law can they assure their survival and prosperity. Until that ideal state is reached, the next best alternative is to work for peace but brace for war.
